stories.headline: Unsealed warrant documents for Ilhan Omar's DC home raid reveal decades-long scope of investigation
stories.note: Newly unsealed records show prosecutors believe Rep. Omar's alleged crimes stretch back decades, keeping a major scandal hanging over House Democrats.
body: Heavily redacted documents behind the search warrant used to raid Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C., home were made public Monday evening, offering the first official look at how wide the federal investigation into the Minnesota Democrat reaches.

In one filing, prosecutors describe the alleged offenses as running from 1980 to the present. Another states plainly that the government believes Omar committed crimes "over decades— beginning long before she was ever in Congress." Fox News Digital has reported that investigators are probing possible immigration fraud tied to how Omar and her late father completed her paperwork after arriving in the U.S. in 1995.

Homeland Security Investigations carried out the Oct. 12 raid, seizing Omar's phone, computer and passport, and authorities also have her DNA. Her sister, Sahra Noor, voluntarily answered investigators' questions that same week. Court filings refer to the congresswoman as "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi," reviving old questions about her 2009 marriage to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi.

Judge James Boasberg, an Obama appointee who had originally agreed to seal the materials, ordered their release after 15 media outlets led by The New York Times, along with Judicial Watch, sued for access. The Justice Department had argued against disclosure. Omar has not been charged with a crime and won a fifth term despite the raid.

Why it matters: The documents make clear this is not a narrow case. A long-running federal probe into one of the most prominent progressive members of Congress is a lasting liability for Democrats as they prepare to take the House majority.

stories.headline: Dem lawmaker to resign after report says he made 'unwelcome' sexual advances toward staffer
stories.note: California Democrat Jimmy Gomez is resigning after a bipartisan Ethics report found his advances toward a young staffer could implicate criminal law.
body: Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., says he will resign from the House on Dec. 1 after the bipartisan House Ethics Committee released a report Monday finding he made "unwelcome" sexual advances toward a congressional staffer.

The committee concluded Gomez knew or should have known his advances, both at a D.C. bar and later in his congressional office, were not welcome, and warned his conduct could implicate D.C. criminal sexual assault laws, including misdemeanor sexual abuse. The woman, in her mid-20s at the time and working for a leadership office, testified about an alleged February 2024 incident at a bar.

The panel also faulted Gomez for ignoring the power imbalance between a member of Congress and a young aide, saying that even if he believed his actions were consensual, that failure fell short of the standards expected of a lawmaker.

Gomez has not been charged and maintains his innocence. When the probe was announced in August, he acknowledged "personal mistakes outside my marriage" but said his relationships were consensual. He was a close ally of former Rep. Eric Swalwell, who also resigned after sexual assault accusations he denied, and founded the Congressional Dads Caucus.
Why it matters: It's another misconduct scandal forcing a Democrat out of Congress, undercutting the party's moral messaging just as it takes control of the House.

stories.headline: Federal judge blocks blue state's ICE mask mandate and other rules targeting federal officers
stories.note: A federal judge blocked Connecticut's rules targeting ICE officers, including a mask ban, as likely unconstitutional, a win for the Trump DOJ.
body: A federal judge has blocked Connecticut from enforcing key parts of a new state law aimed at federal immigration officers, ruling Friday that the provisions likely violate the Constitution.

U.S. District Judge Vernon D. Oliver issued a preliminary injunction against sections of SB 397, passed in May, that set statewide use-of-force standards for federal agents, let state officials investigate and prosecute certain cases involving them, and restricted officers from wearing face coverings. He found those sections likely run afoul of the supremacy clause, which limits states' power over federal operations.

The ruling adds to a string of court losses for state and local efforts to restrict federal officers, following similar decisions in Virginia, New York, Philadelphia and California. It is not a final ruling, and a separate part of the law letting people sue over constitutional violations was not challenged.

Connecticut Democrats pushed back. State Sen. Matt Lesser said he hoped the ruling would be overturned, calling it "un-American to allow masked, secret police to detain our residents." State Rep. Steven Stafstrom said he feared the decision would leave the state less safe and promised to work on next steps.
Why it matters: The decision hands the Justice Department another win and reinforces that blue states can't write their own rules for federal immigration enforcement.

stories.headline: Trump admin announces sweeping measure to cut Iran's 'last financial lifeline'
stories.note: Treasury slapped new sanctions on Iran's 'shadow banking' network, ratcheting up Trump's maximum-pressure campaign on Tehran.
body: The Treasury Department on Monday sanctioned more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, overseas front companies and financial operatives accused of moving billions of dollars through a "shadow banking" network that keeps Iran connected to global trade.

The action by the Office of Foreign Assets Control targets financial channels across Iran, Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey that officials say let Tehran dodge U.S. restrictions, sell oil and petrochemicals, and settle deals in Russian rubles and Chinese yuan. Treasury's FinCEN said it identified about $14.7 billion in activity from January 2025 to August 2026 potentially tied to Iranian shadow banking.

Targets include the Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold, a firm linked to Bank Sarmayeh and three of its officials, two Iran-based currency dealers, and 10 front companies in the UAE, Turkey and Hong Kong. One Dubai firm allegedly handled payments totaling more than $170 million tied to Sadaf Exchange.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called the network "the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime" and vowed to keep dismantling it. The move is the latest step in Operation Economic Outcast, the maximum financial pressure campaign he launched Aug. 24.
Why it matters: As Democrats talk about restricting war funding, the administration is showing it can squeeze Iran's economy hard, a strength-through-pressure contrast Republicans are happy to draw.

stories.headline: Jeffries faces online fury over cryptic answer when asked if Dems would risk gov't shutdown: 'Political games'
stories.note: Incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries wouldn't rule out a government shutdown ahead of the Dec. 11 deadline, giving the GOP an early line of attack.
body: Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is drawing heavy criticism online after refusing to say whether Democrats would risk a government shutdown to get what they want, in an interview with The New York Times.

Asked directly, Jeffries said, "I'm not going to say that one way or the other," explaining that Democrats were still figuring out what's possible in the appropriations process. He said Democrats are weighing restrictions on funding for the Iran war ahead of the Dec. 11 federal funding deadline.

Jeffries also pointed to the 43-day shutdown that began in October 2025 as proof that Democrats won't "go along simply to get along," saying it ended with a forced vote on extending Affordable Care Act tax credits.

Conservatives seized on the clip. RNC Research posted that Jeffries "won't rule out shutting down the government," while other commentators argued Democrats forced shutdowns even in the minority and would find it easier now with majorities in both chambers starting in January.
Why it matters: Before Democrats even take the gavel, their incoming leader is on record leaving a shutdown on the table, which lets Republicans pin the blame in advance if one happens.

stories.headline: Democrats unveil 2028 debate rules with new dark money restrictions — but there's a catch
stories.note: The DNC's new 2028 debate rules make candidates denounce dark money, but enforcement rests largely on self-reporting and skips the general election.
body: The Democratic National Committee released its framework for the 2028 presidential primary on Monday, laying out plans for 12 debates and setting conditions candidates must meet to get on stage.

A headline rule requires candidates to denounce super PAC and 501(c)(4) dark money spending in the primary. The DNC acknowledged it has no legal power to ban those groups, so it is making disavowal a condition of debate qualification instead.

The catch: according to a framework obtained by Fox News Digital, enforcement relies largely on the campaigns themselves. Each must name a liaison to identify and report outside spending; candidates must denounce unapproved spending and refund any they approved or requested. The pledge also covers only the primary, leaving general-election dark money untouched.

Democratic strategist John McCarthy called it "the opening of a conversation" and argued primary voters would punish anyone who refused the pledge. He also said Democrats would be comfortable doing "whatever it takes to win the general election."
Why it matters: The rules let Democrats talk about getting money out of politics while leaving the door wide open once the nominee is chosen, an easy hypocrisy target for Republicans.

stories.headline: States rally behind Catholic church in first-of-its-kind Supreme Court fight over prayer shrine
stories.note: An 18-state coalition led by Kentucky's GOP attorney general is backing a Catholic order at the Supreme Court in a landmark religious liberty case.
body: Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman is leading an 18-state coalition urging the Supreme Court to side with a Catholic religious community blocked from building a small prayer shrine to the Virgin Mary on its own property in Park Hills, Kentucky.

The Missionaries of St. John the Baptist sought approval in 2021 for a 16-by-39-foot grotto, with a plaza and walking path, honoring the apparition at Lourdes. The local zoning board approved it, but neighbors Joel and Elizabeth Frederic sued, and Kentucky's appeals courts ruled against the project. The Kentucky Supreme Court rejected the group's federal religious land-use claim in December 2025.

The justices agreed in October to hear the case, with oral arguments set for Jan. 20, 2027. It is the first time the Court will weigh the land-use protections of the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act, including whether blocking a religious structure is a "substantial burden" on religious exercise.

Coleman said religious liberty "cannot be brushed away simply by a heckler's veto." Ryan Gardner of First Liberty Institute, which represents the Missionaries, has said the case could affect every zoning law in the country.
Why it matters: Republican attorneys general are leading a fight that could strengthen protections for churches nationwide, before a Supreme Court with a conservative majority.
